Q: How do I create a dictionary of dictionaries in Python? A:
  • No need to read the whole file into memory
  • Use batched
  • A list seems more appropriate than dict (like I wrote), then you don't need to track the number manually
from itertools import batched

entries = []
with f:
    for name, line1, line2 in batched(f, 3, strict=True):
        entry = {
            "Name": name.strip(),
            "Line1": line1.strip()
            "Line2": line2.strip()}
        entries.append(entry)

(assuming entry and Sat in your code are empty dicts)

Q: Is order by clause allowed in a subquery A:

In DB2 z/OS there are many reasons for using ORDER BY in a subquery. I have even used it in a subquery of a View where I wanted the default display sequence for SELECT * FROM VIEW to be in a sensible ORDER.

There is little place for academic arguments when it comes to high performance queries. ORDER BY in a subquery can improve the access path, used wisely.

Yes of course, FETCH FIRST n ROWS ONLY, or SKIP FIRST N ROWS has little meaning if data is not ORDERed first. Otherwise random selection of rows, rarely wanted.

Now for nested loop joins, or Correlated EXIST subqueries, if your access path is not choosing a SORT of the outer table, an ORDER BY in subquery could force a sort to help make the query more efficient by index lookaside, reduced data Getpages to next table, or EXISTs Lookaside Cache.

OLAP window function specs have ORDER BY clauses.

GROUP BY and DISTINCT may effectively cause Sorts without ORDER BY, if an index cannot provide that data grouping or duplicate elimination.

Someone mentioned whether ORDER BY allowed in an IN subquery. IN subqueries or NOT IN are highly unadvisable in DB2 z unless DB2 can internally convert to a Join access path, since other access paths can perform quite badly, especially for long IN lists, and sometimes disastrous for correlated IN subqueries. So I use EXISTS (if suitable probe index exists) and JOINs instead (far safer). It may well be that column store DBMSes can handle IN better. My access path expertise is DB2 z/OS and some knowledge for IDAA but limited. Knowing when IN is safe is too complex. Avoid!

So if DB2 lets you do an ORDER BY, and it has a useful purpose, then by all means do so. For Views or subqueries, where ORDER BY is not allowed, this can usually be overcome by using an inner nested subquery with the ORDER BY.

Review of access path can then show if DB2 did anything to use that sequence usefully, or in some cases introduce its own sort of a composite table either defeating your ORDER BY sequence or even re sorting to a different sequence.

If DB2 lets you ORDER BY, then people will do it! No point to say, "should not". It's not one of the cardinal mistakes we see in SQLs that cause big issues, mostly. Would not make the top 20 list of common bad techniques or common faults.

Q: Weird `std::variant::operator==` error with clang + libc++ and specific number of variants A:

It works with -stdlib=libstdc++

It confirms a known category of issues where libc++'s internal implementation of std::variant (specifically the visitation and comparison logic) is not as "recursion-friendly" as libstdc++ (GNU's version)

If you want you can report it.
